Why Did Russia Sell Alaska To The US?

claims.text: On March 30, 1867, Seward agreed to buy Alaska from Russia for $7.2 million, about 2 cents an acre.
claims.quote: on March 30, 1867, agreed to a proposal from Russian Minister in Washington, Edouard de Stoeckl, to purchase Alaska for $7.2 million; or about 2 cents per acre

claims.text: Alexander II, after defeat in the Crimean War, explored selling Alaska, which would be difficult to defend from the United Kingdom in a future war.
claims.quote: having faced a catastrophic defeat in the Crimean War , began exploring the possibility of selling the state's Alaskan possessions, which, in any future war, would be difficult to defend from the United Kingdom; in any future war, it could neither defend nor resupply Alaska, and that Britain could simply take it

claims.text: Russia needed money after being defeated by France and Britain in the Crimean War.
claims.quote: Russia needed money after being defeated by France and Britain in the Crimean War; pitted Russia against Britain, France, and the Ottoman Empire, drained its treasury

claims.text: Permanent Russian settlers in Alaska never numbered more than four hundred.
claims.quote: permanent Russian settlers in Alaska never numbered more than four hundred

claims.text: The purchase added 586,412 square miles; an area over twice as large as Texas.
claims.quote: the United States had grown by 586,412 sq mi; The United States acquired an area over twice as large as Texas; Russia wanted to sell Alaska , all 586,412 square miles of it

claims.text: Skeptics dubbed the purchase 'Seward's Folly'; some called it 'Seward's Icebox'.
claims.quote: Skeptics had dubbed the purchase of Alaska “Seward’s Folly,”; Some opponents labeled the purchase as " Seward's Folly " or " Seward's Icebox "

claims.text: Seward was vindicated when a major gold deposit was found in the Yukon in 1896 and Alaska became the gateway to the Klondike.
claims.quote: was vindicated when a major gold deposit was discovered in the Yukon in 1896, and Alaska became the gateway to the Klondike gold fields

claims.text: Alaska was formally transferred on October 18, 1867.
claims.quote: Alaska was formally transferred to the United States on October 18, 1867

claims.text: The 1867 treaty uses the Diomede islands to mark the US-Russia boundary.
claims.quote: uses the islands to designate the boundary between the two nations; when the United States purchased Alaska from Russia in 1867 and a new border was drawn between the two islands

claims.text: Big Diomede (Russia) and Little Diomede (US) are about 2.4 miles apart.
claims.quote: The two islands are about 2.4 miles; The Russian island Big Diomede was just 2.4 miles in the distance

claims.text: The International Date Line runs between them; Big Diomede is 21 hours ahead of Little Diomede (20 in summer); they are called Tomorrow and Yesterday islands.
claims.quote: Because they are separated by the International Date Line , Big Diomede is almost a day ahead of Little Diomede; Big Diomede is 21 hours ahead of Little Diomede (20 in summer); sometimes called Tomorrow Island (Big Diomede) and Yesterday Island (Little Diomede); The International Date Line (IDL) runs between these islands; Tomorrow Island (Big Diomedes) is 21 hours ahead of Yesterday Isle (Little Diomedes) during standard time

myths.myth: Everyone in America thought the purchase was a joke.
myths.truth: Some critics called it Seward's Folly; the Senate approved it and press opinion was mixed. The script says 'critics called it'.
